questions.question: Which red and buff sandstone is the tallest tower in India built in the thirteenth century?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Qutub Minar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Qutub Minar is the **tallest tower in India**, made of red and buff sandstone, and was commissioned in the late 12th century.
 
• It was initiated by **Qutb-ud-din Aibak**, the founder of the Delhi Sultanate, and later completed by his successor, Iltutmish.
 
• The tower is located in **Delhi, India**, and is a prominent UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
• It stands at a height of **73 meters (240 feet)** and consists of five tapering stories.
 
• Qutub Minar is adorned with intricate carvings and verses from the Quran, showcasing the Indo-Islamic architectural style.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Qutub Minar Complex:**

 
 
• The Qutub Minar is part of the larger Qutub Complex, which includes structures like the Alai Darwaza, Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, and the Iron Pillar.
 
• The Iron Pillar, located within the complex, is a marvel of metallurgical skills and is known for its rust-resistant properties.
 
 
 
• **Architectural Significance:**
 
 
• The tower represents the Indo-Islamic architectural style, blending Persian, Afghan, and Indian designs.
 
• The first three stories are made of red sandstone, while the fourth and fifth stories are constructed using marble and sandstone.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• Qutub Minar was built to commemorate the victory of Qutb-ud-din Aibak over the last Hindu kingdom in Delhi.
 
• It also served as a symbol of the beginning of Muslim rule in India.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Status:**
 
 
• The Qutub Minar and its monuments were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in **1993**.
 
• The site attracts millions of tourists annually and is one of the most visited monuments in India.

questions.question: The people of Himachal Pradesh make channels to bring water from a glacier or rainwater to villages for the function of mainly irrigation. These channels are locally known as:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Guls or Kuls**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Guls or Kuls** are traditional water channels used in Himachal Pradesh to divert water from glaciers or rainwater to villages for irrigation and other agricultural purposes.
 
• These channels are constructed using locally available materials like mud, stones, and wood, making them cost-effective and sustainable.
 
• The water is distributed evenly across fields through a network of small channels, ensuring efficient irrigation in hilly terrains.
 
• Guls or Kuls have been used for centuries in the region and are an excellent example of traditional water management systems in India.
 
• They are primarily found in the mountainous regions of Himachal Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir, where agriculture heavily depends on glacial meltwater and rainfall.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Khadins**

 
 
• Khadins are traditional water harvesting systems found in Rajasthan.
 
• They consist of a bund (embankment) built across a slope to capture surface runoff and allow it to percolate into the ground.
 
• They are used for both irrigation and groundwater recharge in arid and semi-arid regions.
 
 
 
• **Johads**
 
 
• Johads are small earthen check dams constructed to collect and store rainwater.
 
• They are primarily found in Rajasthan and other parts of northwestern India.
 
• Johads help in increasing groundwater levels and are used for drinking water and irrigation purposes.
 
 
 
• **Baori**
 
 
• Baoris are stepwells found in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
 
• They serve as water storage systems and are known for their architectural beauty.
 
• These structures provide water for drinking and other daily activities, especially during the dry season.
 
 
 
• **Traditional Water Management in India**
 
 
• India has a rich tradition of indigenous water management systems adapted to local climatic and geographical conditions.
 
• Examples include Zabo (Nagaland), Bamboo Drip Irrigation (Meghalaya), and Eri (Tamil Nadu).
 
• These systems emphasize sustainability, community participation, and efficient use of resources.

questions.question: In which year was the microfinance movement formally launched in India on a pilot basis?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1992**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The microfinance movement in India was formally launched in **1992** on a pilot basis by the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD).
 
• This initiative focused on linking **Self-Help Groups (SHGs)** to banks, enabling better access to financial services for the rural poor.
 
• It aimed to provide **credit and savings facilities** to people in rural areas who lacked access to formal financial institutions.
 
• The **Self-Help Group-Bank Linkage Program (SHG-BLP)** was the cornerstone of this microfinance movement in India.
 
• By the end of the 1990s, this model of microfinance gained momentum and became one of the largest microfinance initiatives globally.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Self-Help Groups (SHGs):**

 
 
• SHGs are informal associations of people who come together to address common financial and social issues.
 
• They pool small savings from members and use the funds for lending within the group.
 
• SHGs play a vital role in promoting financial inclusion and women's empowerment in rural India.
 
 
 
• **NABARD:**
 
 
• The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) is a development bank focused on rural development in India.
 
• It was established in **1982** to provide credit and financial support to agriculture and rural sectors.
 
• NABARD spearheads several programs, including the SHG-BLP, to promote financial inclusion.
 
 
 
• **Microfinance:**
 
 
• Microfinance refers to providing financial services like loans, savings, and insurance to the economically disadvantaged.
 
• It aims to reduce poverty and empower individuals by enabling them to become financially self-sufficient.
 
• Globally, organizations like Grameen Bank in Bangladesh are known pioneers of microfinance.
 
 
 
• **Significance of SHG-BLP:**
 
 
• The SHG-Bank Linkage Program has been instrumental in extending financial services to millions in rural India.
 
• It is one of the largest microfinance programs globally, involving commercial banks, regional rural banks, and cooperative banks.
 
• The program has contributed significantly to poverty alleviation and rural development.

questions.question: Who among the following founded a suburban township near Vijayanagara, called Nagalapuram, after his mother?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Krishna Deva Raya**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Krishna Deva Raya** was a prominent ruler of the Vijayanagara Empire who reigned from 1509 to 1529.
 
• He founded the suburban township of **Nagalapuram** in honor of his mother, Nagala Devi.
 
• Krishna Deva Raya was known for his administrative prowess, military strength, and contributions to art, culture, and architecture in South India.
 
• The Vijayanagara Empire flourished under his rule, becoming a major center for trade, culture, and religion.
 
• He also authored the Telugu literary work **Amuktamalyada**, showcasing his deep interest in literature and spirituality.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vijayanagara Empire:**

 
 
• The Vijayanagara Empire, established in 1336, was one of the most significant South Indian empires, known for its contributions to art, architecture, and economy.
 
• It served as a bulwark against Islamic invasions in South India and fostered a synthesis of Hindu culture and traditions.
 
• Hampi, the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire, is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
 
 
• **Krishna Deva Raya's Achievements:**
 
 
• He expanded the empire's territory through military campaigns, including victories over the Bahmani Sultanate and the Gajapati rulers of Odisha.
 
• His reign marked a golden age of prosperity, with advancements in trade, agriculture, and irrigation systems.
 
• He patronized several temples, including the famous Virupaksha Temple in Hampi.
 
 
 
• **Amuktamalyada:**
 
 
• Written in Telugu, Amuktamalyada is a poetic work by Krishna Deva Raya that narrates the story of the Tamil saint Andal.
 
• The text reflects his deep devotion to Lord Vishnu and his intellectual engagement with literature and spiritual philosophy.
 
 
 
• **Nagalapuram:**
 
 
• Nagalapuram, named after Nagala Devi (Krishna Deva Raya's mother), is located in present-day Andhra Pradesh.
 
• The town showcases the architectural and cultural advancements of the Vijayanagara Empire.

questions.question: In which sport is the term 'Dolphin Kick' commonly used?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Swimming**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The term 'Dolphin Kick' refers to a specific swimming technique primarily used in **competitive swimming**, especially in the butterfly stroke and underwater phases of other strokes.
 
• This kick involves a fluid, wave-like motion of the legs and hips, similar to the movement of a dolphin's tail.
 
• The 'Dolphin Kick' is considered one of the fastest ways to propel underwater and is often used during starts and turns in freestyle, backstroke, and butterfly events.
 
• Swimmers use core muscles to generate the wave motion, which starts at the hips and flows down to the feet for maximum propulsion.
 
• This technique plays a vital role in competitive swimming, as mastering it can lead to significant improvements in speed and performance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Butterfly Stroke:**

 
 
• The butterfly stroke is one of the four main swimming strokes used in competitive swimming.
 
• It is characterized by a simultaneous movement of both arms in a circular motion and the use of the 'Dolphin Kick' for leg propulsion.
 
• This stroke requires a high level of coordination and strength, making it one of the most challenging swimming techniques.
 
 
 
• **Underwater Phase:**
 
 
• The underwater phase occurs immediately after a swimmer dives or completes a turn.
 
• During this phase, swimmers often use the 'Dolphin Kick' to maximize speed before surfacing.
 
• Rules in competitive swimming, such as FINA regulations, limit the distance swimmers can stay underwater to 15 meters after starts and turns.
 
 
 
• **Core Strength in Swimming:**
 
 
• Core strength is crucial for generating the wave-like motion required in the 'Dolphin Kick.'
 
• Strong abdominal and lower back muscles help swimmers maintain efficient and powerful movements.
 
• Exercises like planks and leg raises are commonly used to improve core strength among swimmers.
 
 
 
• **Competitive Swimming Rules:**
 
 
• FINA, the international governing body for swimming, establishes rules for strokes, starts, and turns in competitions.
 
• The 'Dolphin Kick' is regulated to ensure fair play, and swimmers must surface within 15 meters after starts or turns.
 
• Mastering the 'Dolphin Kick' while adhering to these rules can give swimmers a competitive edge.

questions.question: Which of the following novels is based on Malgudi, a fictional town in south India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Guide**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **The Guide**, written by R.K. Narayan, is one of the most celebrated novels in Indian English literature.
 
• The novel is set in the fictional town of **Malgudi**, which serves as the backdrop for many of R.K. Narayan's works.
 
• Malgudi is a fictional South Indian town created by R.K. Narayan to depict everyday life in a small Indian town.
 
• **The Guide** won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1960, making R.K. Narayan one of the first Indian authors to receive the honor.
 
• The book was adapted into a critically acclaimed Bollywood movie, **Guide**, in 1965, starring Dev Anand and Waheeda Rehman.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **R.K. Narayan:**

 
 
• R.K. Narayan (1906-2001) is one of the pioneers of Indian English literature.
 
• He is known for his simple yet profound storytelling, often rooted in Indian culture and traditions.
 
• His other notable works include **Swami and Friends**, **The Bachelor of Arts**, and **The English Teacher**.
 
 
 
• **Malgudi:**
 
 
• Malgudi is a fictional town created by R.K. Narayan to reflect the essence of a typical South Indian town.
 
• The town combines Indian traditions with modernity, serving as a microcosm of Indian society.
 
• It first appeared in his novel **Swami and Friends** (1935).
 
 
 
• **The Guide - Themes:**
 
 
• The novel explores themes like personal transformation, love, greed, and spirituality.
 
• The protagonist, Raju, evolves from being a tourist guide to a spiritual leader in the story.
 
 
 
• **Indian English Literature:**
 
 
• Indian English literature refers to works written by Indian authors in the English language.
 
• Prominent authors include R.K. Narayan, Mulk Raj Anand, Raja Rao, and more recently, Arundhati Roy and Salman Rushdie.
 
• It often highlights Indian traditions, societal changes, and historical events.

questions.question: In which of the following years did India NOT win an Olympic gold medal in hockey?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1960**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• India's hockey team dominated the Olympics during the mid-20th century, winning six consecutive gold medals between 1928 and 1956.
 
• India won gold medals in Olympic hockey in the years **1948 (London), 1952 (Helsinki), and 1956 (Melbourne)**.
 
• In the 1960 Rome Olympics, India lost the final match to Pakistan, ending their streak of gold medal victories.
 
• This marked the first time India did not win a gold medal in hockey since their first victory in 1928.
 
• India regained the Olympic hockey gold medal in 1964 at the Tokyo Olympics.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian Hockey Dominance:**

 
 
• India won its first Olympic hockey gold medal in 1928 in Amsterdam and went on to win six consecutive golds until 1956.
 
• Indian hockey legends like Dhyan Chand played pivotal roles during this golden era.
 
 
 
• **1960 Rome Olympics Hockey Final:**
 
 
• India lost 1-0 to Pakistan in the final match, marking a historic defeat.
 
• Pakistan's victory in 1960 was the first time any team had broken India’s streak in Olympic hockey.
 
 
 
• **India's Hockey Legacy:**
 
 
• India has won a total of eight Olympic gold medals in hockey, the most by any country.
 
• The team remained a dominant force in international hockey until the late 20th century.
 
 
 
• **Revival Efforts:**
 
 
• After a decline in performance, India won its first Olympic hockey medal in 41 years (bronze) at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics.
 
• The Indian hockey team continues to work towards regaining its status as a global powerhouse.

questions.question: Which of the following states is characterised by salt marshes known as 'Rann'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Rann of Kutch** in Gujarat is one of the largest salt marshes in the world.
 
• It is located in the **Thar Desert** and spans approximately **7,500 square kilometers**.
 
• The area is famous for its seasonal salt marshes, which remain submerged during the monsoon and dry up to form salt flats during the dry season.
 
• The Rann of Kutch is divided into two parts: **Great Rann of Kutch** and **Little Rann of Kutch**.
 
• It is known for the **Rann Utsav**, a cultural festival showcasing Gujarat's heritage, held annually during winter.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Salt Marshes**:

 
 
• Salt marshes are coastal wetlands inundated by tides and dominated by salt-tolerant plants.
 
• They play a crucial role in maintaining ecological balance by serving as habitats for diverse flora and fauna.
 
 
 
• **Thar Desert**:
 
 
• The Thar Desert is the 17th largest desert in the world and spans parts of India and Pakistan.
 
• It is characterized by extreme temperatures, scant rainfall, and unique biodiversity.
 
 
 
• **Rann Utsav**:
 
 
• Rann Utsav is an annual cultural festival organized by the Gujarat government.
 
• It features folk music, dance performances, adventure sports, and handicrafts.
 
• The event attracts visitors globally and celebrates the rich heritage of Gujarat.
 
 
 
• **Unique Biodiversity**:
 
 
• The Rann of Kutch is home to the endangered Indian Wild Ass, found in the Little Rann of Kutch.
 
• The region also hosts migratory birds such as flamingos and pelicans during the winter season.

questions.question: Who among the following wrote a book called 'Indica' based on his travels and experiences in Mauryan India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Megasthenes**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Megasthenes** was a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus I Nicator to the Mauryan court of Emperor Chandragupta Maurya in the 4th century BCE.
 
• He authored the book **'Indica'**, which provides a detailed account of Mauryan India, including its geography, society, economy, and governance.
 
• The work of Megasthenes is considered one of the earliest known written accounts of India by a foreign traveler, offering valuable historical insights.
 
• 'Indica' has not survived in its entirety, but fragments and references to it are found in the writings of later authors like Strabo, Arrian, and Diodorus.
 
• His observations on the Mauryan administration, the caste system, and the city of Pataliputra are particularly notable for historians.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indica and Its Legacy:**

 
 
• 'Indica' was a pioneering ethnographic work that provided a foreign perspective on ancient India.
 
• Although the original text is lost, its content has been preserved through citations by later Greek and Roman historians.
 
 
 
• **Megasthenes' Contributions:**
 
 
• He described the administrative efficiency of the Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya.
 
• His account includes details about Pataliputra (modern-day Patna), the empire's capital, which he compared to the grandeur of cities like Susa and Babylon.
 
 
 
• **Relations Between Greece and Mauryan India:**
 
 
• Megasthenes' visit highlights the diplomatic ties between the Mauryan Empire and the Hellenistic world following Alexander the Great's campaigns.
 
• Seleucus I Nicator, a Hellenistic ruler, sent Megasthenes to Chandragupta's court as part of a treaty agreement.
 
 
 
• **Other Ancient Travelers to India:**
 
 
• Other notable foreign accounts of ancient India include those by Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang, and Al-Biruni, who provided rich insights into Indian culture and history.

questions.question: In which of the following states is the Jawara dance performed on the occasion of a successful harvest?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madhya Pradesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Jawara dance** is a traditional folk dance performed in the state of **Madhya Pradesh**.
 
• This dance is predominantly performed during the celebration of a **successful harvest**, symbolizing joy and prosperity.
 
• The performers often carry **jawara (harvested crops)** on their heads while dancing, showcasing the importance of agriculture in their lives.
 
• Jawara dance is usually performed in rural areas and is accompanied by **traditional folk music** and vibrant costumes.
 
• The dance reflects the cultural essence of Madhya Pradesh and highlights its **agrarian roots**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Folk Dances of Madhya Pradesh**

 
 
• Other prominent folk dances of Madhya Pradesh include **Tertali, Matki, Phulpati, and Grida.**
 
• These dances are performed on various occasions such as festivals, weddings, and cultural celebrations.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Harvest Festivals**
 
 
• Harvest festivals like those celebrated through Jawara dance are a way to **express gratitude to nature** for a bountiful yield.
 
• They also serve as a platform to **strengthen community bonds** and preserve cultural heritage.
 
 
 
• **Agriculture in Madhya Pradesh**
 
 
• Madhya Pradesh is known as the **"Soybean State of India"** and is a significant contributor to India's agricultural economy.
 
• Wheat, rice, maize, and pulses are other major crops grown in the state.
 
 
 
• **Traditional Attire in Jawara Dance**
 
 
• The dancers wear **vividly colored traditional outfits**, which add to the vibrancy of the performance.
 
• Women often adorn themselves with intricate jewelry and ornaments.

questions.question: Who among the following was a leader of Garam Dal, a group of radical nationalists?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bipin Chandra Pal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Bipin Chandra Pal was one of the prominent leaders of the **Garam Dal** (Extremist faction) of the Indian National Congress.
 
• He was part of the famous triumvirate known as the **Lal-Bal-Pal trio**, which included Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bipin Chandra Pal.
 
• The Garam Dal emphasized **direct action and self-reliance**, rejecting the moderate approach of petitions and prayers advocated by the Naram Dal (Moderates).
 
• Bipin Chandra Pal was a staunch advocate of **Swadeshi (use of Indian-made goods)** and Swaraj (self-rule).
 
• He played a significant role in the **Swadeshi Movement** of 1905, which was launched in response to the partition of Bengal by Lord Curzon.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Garam Dal vs Naram Dal:**

 
 
• The Garam Dal (Extremists) advocated radical methods, including boycotts, protests, and mass mobilization, while the Naram Dal (Moderates) believed in dialogue and constitutional means.
 
• The split between the two factions became evident during the Surat Session of the Indian National Congress in 1907.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement:**
 
 
• Launched in 1905, it aimed at promoting Indian goods and boycotting British products to strengthen India's economy.
 
• Bipin Chandra Pal actively campaigned for the movement through public speeches and writings.
 
 
 
• **Lal-Bal-Pal:**
 
 
• This trio of leaders symbolized the extremist phase of the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and Bipin Chandra Pal were committed to achieving self-rule through assertive and revolutionary methods.
 
 
 
• **Partition of Bengal (1905):**
 
 
• Introduced by Lord Curzon, it divided Bengal into East and West regions, ostensibly for administrative efficiency but largely to weaken nationalist sentiments.
 
• The decision faced massive opposition, leading to the rise of the Swadeshi and Boycott movements.
 
 
 
• **Bipin Chandra Pal’s Contributions:**
 
 
• He was a writer, orator, and journalist who used his skills to inspire nationalist fervor.
 
• His publications included "New India" and "The Indian People," where he promoted his vision for an independent India.

questions.question: Who among the following presides over the meeting of the Council of Ministers in a state?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Chief Minister of the state**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Chief Minister is the **head of the Council of Ministers** in a state and presides over its meetings.
 
• The Chief Minister plays a pivotal role in shaping policies and ensuring coordination among ministers for governance.
 
• All major decisions of the Council of Ministers are deliberated and finalized under the leadership of the Chief Minister.
 
• As the executive authority of the state, the Chief Minister ensures the implementation of government policies and programs.
 
• The Governor appoints the Chief Minister, who is usually the leader of the majority party in the Legislative Assembly.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Council of Ministers:**

 
 
• The Council of Ministers includes the Chief Minister, Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State, and Deputy Ministers.
 
• It collectively exercises executive power and advises the Governor on various matters.
 
• It is responsible for the formulation and execution of policies in the state.
 
 
 
• **Governor:**
 
 
• The Governor is the constitutional head of the state and acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
 
• The Governor's role is largely ceremonial, but they play a key role in appointing the Chief Minister.
 
 
 
• **Legislative Assembly:**
 
 
• The Legislative Assembly is the primary law-making body in the state.
 
• The Chief Minister is usually the leader of the majority party in the Legislative Assembly.
 
• It is responsible for passing laws and budgets for the state.
 
 
 
• **Executive Authority:**
 
 
• The Chief Minister holds the real executive authority in the state.
 
• He/she is responsible for the day-to-day functioning of the state government.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of mesosomes?

options.text: Increase the surface area of the plasma membrane and enzymatic content
DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Locomotion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Mesosomes** are invaginations or inward foldings of the plasma membrane in prokaryotic cells, primarily observed in bacteria.
 
• The primary functions of mesosomes include **increasing the surface area of the plasma membrane** for enzymatic activity and facilitating cellular processes such as respiration.
 
• Mesosomes play a crucial role in **DNA replication** and ensuring proper distribution of DNA to daughter cells during cell division.
 
• They also assist in the formation of the cell wall during bacterial cell division.
 
• **Locomotion** is not a function of mesosomes, as bacterial locomotion is mediated by structures like flagella, not mesosomes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mesosomes in Prokaryotes:**

 
 
• Mesosomes are more prominent in gram-positive bacteria and are less commonly observed in gram-negative bacteria.
 
• They are thought to play a role in the compartmentalization of metabolic activities within the bacterial cell.
 
 
 
• **Cellular Respiration in Bacteria:**
 
 
• In prokaryotic cells, the plasma membrane, including mesosomes, contains enzymes necessary for cellular respiration and ATP synthesis.
 
• Unlike eukaryotes, bacteria lack mitochondria, so mesosomes help compensate by increasing membrane surface area for these processes.
 
 
 
• **Structures Involved in Locomotion:**
 
 
• Bacterial locomotion is facilitated by the **flagella**, which are long, whip-like structures made of the protein flagellin.
 
• Other structures like pili or fimbriae are involved in adhesion but not in locomotion.
 
 
 
• **Bacterial Cell Division:**
 
 
• Mesosomes are believed to be associated with the segregation of replicated DNA and the formation of the septum during binary fission in bacterial cells.
 
• They play a structural and organizational role during the process of cytokinesis.

questions.question: Who was sworn in as the Governor of Chhattisgarh in February 2023?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Biswabhusan Harichandan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

questions.question: Which of the following Khayal artists is the founding father of Lalit Kala Kendra of the University of Pune?
questions.solution:

__
 
• Pandit **Bhimsen Joshi**, a legendary Hindustani classical vocalist, is widely regarded as one of the greatest Khayal singers of India.
 
• He was instrumental in the establishment of **Lalit Kala Kendra**, the Centre for Performing Arts, at the University of Pune.
 
• Bhimsen Joshi was known for his unique blend of traditional ragas with an innovative approach, which made him a pioneer of modern Khayal singing.
 
• He was a recipient of several prestigious awards, including the **Bharat Ratna** (2008), India's highest civilian award, and the Padma Vibhushan (1999).
 
• His contributions to Hindustani classical music have left a lasting legacy, inspiring generations of musicians and music enthusiasts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Khayal Music**

 
 
• Khayal is a form of Hindustani classical music that emphasizes improvisation and emotional expression.
 
• It is characterized by its two main sections: the slow tempo "Vilambit" and the fast tempo "Drut."
 
• Khayal singing often incorporates intricate ornamentation and raga exploration.
 
 
 
• **Lalit Kala Kendra**
 
 
• Lalit Kala Kendra, established by Bhimsen Joshi, is a prestigious institute for performing arts education in Pune.
 
• It offers specialized training in various traditional Indian art forms, including classical music, dance, and drama.
 
• The center aims to preserve and promote India's rich cultural heritage.
 
 
 
• **Bharat Ratna Award**
 
 
• The Bharat Ratna is India's highest civilian award, conferred for exceptional service in art, literature, science, and public service.
 
• Bhimsen Joshi received the Bharat Ratna in 2008 for his unparalleled contributions to Indian music.
 
 
 
• **Hindustani Classical Music Gharanas**
 
 
• Gharanas are schools or styles of Hindustani classical music, each with unique characteristics and techniques.
 
• Bhimsen Joshi belonged to the **Kirana Gharana**, known for its emphasis on melody and emotional depth.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a hydroelectric power plant?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sambhar Lake Hydel Project**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Sambhar Lake** is India’s largest inland saltwater lake located in Rajasthan and is primarily used for salt production, not for hydroelectric power generation.
 
• Hydroelectric power plants utilize flowing water to generate electricity, typically requiring dams or significant water flow, which Sambhar Lake lacks.
 
• Other listed projects like **Bhakra Nangal**, **Damodar Valley**, and **Kopili Hydel Project** are well-known hydroelectric power plants in India.
 
• Sambhar Lake is significant for its ecological and economic value but does not contribute to India’s hydroelectric power infrastructure.
 
• Hydroelectric power plants are typically located in regions with ample freshwater resources and elevation changes, which Sambhar Lake does not possess.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hydroelectric Power:**

 
 
• Hydroelectric power is the generation of electricity using water flow through turbines.
 
• It is a renewable energy source that contributes significantly to India’s energy mix.
 
• India has several major hydropower projects including Bhakra Nangal, Tehri Dam, and Sardar Sarovar Dam.
 
 
 
• **Sambhar Lake:**
 
 
• Located in Rajasthan, Sambhar Lake spans over 190 square kilometers.
 
• It is a Ramsar site, recognized for its ecological importance and migratory bird habitats.
 
• The lake is a major contributor to India’s salt production but lacks infrastructure for electricity generation.
 
 
 
• **Bhakra Nangal Hydel Project:**
 
 
• Situated on the Sutlej River, this project is one of India’s largest hydropower facilities.
 
• It serves multiple purposes, including electricity generation, irrigation, and flood control.
 
 
 
• **Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC):**
 
 
• Established in 1948, DVC operates several hydropower and thermal power plants.
 
• Its hydropower plants are located in Jharkhand and West Bengal.

questions.question: Which of the following is an alarming effect of thermal pollution in water bodies?

options.text: The amount of dissolved oxygen decreased significantly
The random changes in pH values

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The amount of dissolved oxygen decreased significantly**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Thermal pollution increases the temperature of water bodies, which reduces the solubility of oxygen in water.
 
• Lower levels of dissolved oxygen negatively impact aquatic organisms, disrupting their respiration and survival mechanisms.
 
• Decreased dissolved oxygen can lead to hypoxic conditions, causing mass deaths of fish and other aquatic life.
 
• Warm water also accelerates the metabolic rates of aquatic organisms, increasing their oxygen demand while simultaneously reducing oxygen availability.
 
• Thermal pollution is often caused by industrial discharges, such as cooling water from power plants, or urban runoff that raises water temperatures.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Thermal Pollution:**

 
 
• Thermal pollution occurs when industries discharge heated water or effluents into natural water bodies, altering the temperature balance.
 
• It negatively impacts aquatic ecosystems by disrupting breeding patterns, migration cycles, and biodiversity.
 
• Sources include power plants, manufacturing industries, deforestation, and urban runoff.
 
 
 
• **Dissolved Oxygen (DO):**
 
 
• Dissolved oxygen refers to the amount of oxygen present in water, essential for the survival of aquatic organisms.
 
• DO levels are inversely proportional to water temperature – higher temperatures reduce oxygen solubility.
 
• Low DO levels can lead to hypoxic conditions, affecting aquatic biodiversity and ecosystem health.
 
 
 
• **Hypoxia:**
 
 
• Hypoxia refers to oxygen deficiency in water, often caused by thermal pollution or organic matter decomposition.
 
• It can result in dead zones where aquatic life struggles to survive, such as areas in the Gulf of Mexico.
 
• Hypoxia disrupts food chains and aquatic ecosystems, leading to significant ecological damage.
 
 
 
• **Control Measures:**
 
 
• Cooling ponds, cooling towers, and heat exchangers can be used to minimize thermal pollution.
 
• Planting vegetation along water bodies helps reduce temperature fluctuations and runoff impacts.
 
• Regulating industrial discharges through environmental laws ensures better temperature management in water bodies.

questions.question: According to National Multidimensional Poverty Index 2023 (A Progress Review), what was the proportion of population in multidimensional poverty (Headcount Ratio) in rural India in 2019-2021?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**19.28%**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) 2023 measures multidimensional poverty using three dimensions: **health, education, and standard of living**.
 
• As per the report, **19.28%** (or 0.1928) of the rural population in India was living in multidimensional poverty during the period 2019–2021.
 
• This represents a significant reduction in rural multidimensional poverty compared to previous years, reflecting the impact of various poverty alleviation schemes.
 
• The MPI considers multiple deprivations that individuals face simultaneously, including indicators like nutrition, child mortality, schooling, and access to clean water and electricity.
 
• The data was released by NITI Aayog, which is responsible for tracking and reporting poverty statistics in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI):**

 
 
• The MPI is based on the **global methodology developed by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI).
 
• It includes indicators across three dimensions: health (nutrition, child mortality), education (years of schooling, school attendance), and standard of living (access to cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets).
 
• The index provides a more comprehensive view of poverty than income-based measures alone.
 
 
 
• **Rural vs. Urban Poverty:**
 
 
• Rural poverty in India has historically been higher than urban poverty due to limited access to education, healthcare, and infrastructure in rural areas.
 
• Government schemes like **Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana, Saubhagya Scheme, and Jal Jeevan Mission** have significantly contributed to poverty alleviation in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Significance of MPI:**
 
 
• MPI serves as a tool to monitor progress towards achieving the **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)**, particularly Goal 1: No Poverty.
 
• It helps policymakers identify and address specific areas of deprivation in populations.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• India’s improvement in MPI contributes to the global reduction of multidimensional poverty, given its large population.
 
• The MPI approach has been adopted by many countries to track multidimensional poverty at national and subnational levels.

questions.question: Who among the following was the founder of 'Bhoodan Yajna' in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vinoba Bhave**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Vinoba Bhave** was the founder of the **Bhoodan Yajna**, a land donation movement in India.
 
• The movement was initiated in **1951** at Pochampally village in Telangana, where Bhave convinced wealthy landowners to donate land to landless peasants.
 
• The primary aim of Bhoodan was to address **land redistribution** and reduce socio-economic inequality in rural India.
 
• Vinoba Bhave was a follower of **Mahatma Gandhi** and believed in achieving social justice through non-violence and persuasion.
 
• The Bhoodan Movement was a significant part of India's post-independence **Sarvodaya movement**, which aimed for the welfare of all.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Bhoodan Yajna:**

 
 
• Bhoodan translates to "land donation," and the movement was aimed at redistributing land from wealthy landowners to the landless.
 
• It was a voluntary initiative that relied on moral persuasion rather than force or legislation.
 
• The movement later evolved into the **Gramdan Movement**, where entire villages collectively donated land.
 
 
 
• **Vinoba Bhave:**
 
 
• Vinoba Bhave (1895–1982) was a prominent social reformer and a staunch follower of Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• He was the first recipient of the **Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership** in 1958.
 
• He believed in non-violent methods to achieve social and economic equity.
 
 
 
• **Sarvodaya Movement:**
 
 
• The Sarvodaya Movement, meaning "progress for all," was inspired by Gandhian principles.
 
• It aimed at social transformation through self-reliance, non-violence, and grassroots development.
 
• Bhoodan Yajna was one of the key components of the larger Sarvodaya Movement.
 
 
 
• **Pochampally:**
 
 
• Pochampally, where the Bhoodan Movement was initiated, is now known as **Pochampally Handloom Park** and is famous for its handwoven Ikat sarees.
 
• The village is located in the Yadadri Bhuvanagiri district of Telangana.

questions.question: Which part of a flower develops into a seed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ovule**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **ovule** is the part of the flower that develops into a seed after fertilization.
 
• It is located within the ovary of the pistil, which is the female reproductive part of the flower.
 
• After fertilization, the ovule matures into a seed, while the ovary develops into a fruit.
 
• The seed contains the plant embryo along with stored food, which is essential for germination and growth.
 
• Each ovule consists of protective layers (integuments) and a central tissue called the nucellus, where the embryo sac is formed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Parts of a Flower:**

 
 
• The flower is composed of four main parts: sepals, petals, stamens (male reproductive organs), and pistils (female reproductive organs).
 
• The pistil consists of three main parts: stigma, style, and ovary, where the ovules are housed.
 
 
 
• **Pollination and Fertilization:**
 
 
• Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther (male part) to the stigma (female part).
 
• Fertilization occurs when the male gamete in the pollen fuses with the female gamete in the ovule, forming a zygote.
 
 
 
• **Seed Development:**
 
 
• After fertilization, the zygote develops into an embryo, and the ovule transforms into a seed.
 
• The seed coat develops from the integuments of the ovule, providing protection to the embryo.
 
 
 
• **Fruit Formation:**
 
 
• While the ovule becomes the seed, the ovary of the flower develops into a fruit that protects the seeds and aids in their dispersal.

questions.question:
Which Article of the Indian Constitution states the following?

‘Directive Principles of State Policy are fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the state to apply these principles in making laws.’
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 37**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 37** of the Indian Constitution states that Directive Principles of State Policy are fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
• The article emphasizes that it is the **duty of the state to apply these principles** while making laws.
 
• Directive Principles are **non-justiciable**, meaning they cannot be enforced by courts, but they serve as guiding principles for the state.
 
• These principles aim to establish a welfare state by promoting social and economic justice.
 
• Article 37 acts as a bridge between the ideals enshrined in the Constitution and the practical steps taken by the state for governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP):**

 
 
• DPSP are enshrined in Part IV of the Indian Constitution (Articles 36-51).
 
• They were inspired by the Irish Constitution and aim to establish socio-economic democracy.
 
• Examples include promoting equal pay for equal work, improving public health, and ensuring free legal aid.
 
• They are not enforceable by law but act as fundamental guidelines for governance.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights vs Directive Principles:**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights (Part III) are enforceable by courts, while Directive Principles are not.
 
• In case of conflict, the judiciary generally prioritizes Fundamental Rights.
 
• However, efforts have been made to harmonize both for balanced governance (e.g., through constitutional amendments).
 
 
 
• **Welfare State Concept:**
 
 
• The Directive Principles aim to achieve the concept of a welfare state in India.
 
• A welfare state seeks to ensure social equity, economic justice, and the upliftment of marginalized sections of society.
 
• Examples include policies for poverty alleviation, education, and public health.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Interpretation:**
 
 
• Indian courts have emphasized the importance of DPSP in landmark cases like Minerva Mills (1980) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
 
• These cases highlighted the role of DPSP in achieving the goals set by the Constitution.

• It commemorates the **divine marriage of Lord Krishna and Rukmini**, which is believed to have taken place in Madhavpur Ghed, a coastal village in Gujarat.
 
• The fair showcases **cultural integration between Gujarat and the northeastern states**, particularly Arunachal Pradesh, where Rukmini is revered as a princess of the Idu Mishmi tribe.
 
• Organized by the Government of Gujarat, the event features **folk dance performances, art exhibitions, and spiritual processions**.
 
• The Madhavpur Fair is also significant for **promoting India’s cultural heritage** and fostering unity through spiritual and traditional celebrations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rukmini’s Connection to Arunachal Pradesh:** Rukmini is believed to belong to the Idu Mishmi tribe from Arunachal Pradesh, symbolizing a strong cultural bond between the region and Gujarat.
 
• **Historical and Mythological Significance:** According to mythology, Lord Krishna married Rukmini after eloping with her from her hometown, which is celebrated during the fair.
 
• **Government Initiative:** The fair is supported by the Ministry of Culture and the Government of Gujarat to **revive and celebrate India’s traditional heritage**.
 
• **Cultural Events:** The fair includes a variety of activities such as **traditional music performances, art displays, and religious ceremonies** to attract tourists and devotees.
 
• **Tourism Boost:** The Madhavpur Ghed Fair plays a vital role in **boosting cultural tourism** in Gujarat, drawing visitors from across India and abroad.
